explanations.explanation: Slaves is the word Paul uses. Paul is the apostle writing this letter, and he says before they knew God, “…you were slaves to those who by nature are not gods.” That's a heavy word, and he picked it on purpose. Now you see why what comes next matters so much to him.

Strangers sounds soft, but it's not Paul's word. Paul is the apostle writing this letter, and he says they “were slaves.” A stranger just walks past you. A slave is owned, and Paul wants the Galatians to feel the difference.

Neighbors are the folks who borrow your ladder and return it three weeks later. That's not the picture Paul paints. Paul is the apostle writing this letter, and he says that before they knew God, they were slaves to those who by nature are not gods. Much heavier than a ladder.

explanations.answer: Going back to weak and worthless principles
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul asks, “…how is it that you are turning back to those weak and worthless principles?” Notice the words turning back. They already know God, and Paul is stunned they'd walk toward something that held them before. I think he asks it because he can't believe it.

explanations.answer: Chasing after rich and powerful friends
explanations.explanation: Rich and powerful friends never show up in this passage. Paul says they're turning back to “weak and worthless principles.” Those are the very things that once held them in slavery. The trouble here isn't a fancy guest list.

explanations.answer: Arguing over small and petty disputes
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention any petty arguments here. What he says is that they're turning back to “those weak and worthless principles” (Galatians 4:9). Then he asks if they want to be enslaved by them all over again. That's a much bigger worry than a squabble.

True. Paul asks, “Do you wish to be enslaved by them all over again?” It's a question, and I think he asks it so they'll stop and look at where they're headed. Nobody picks slavery on purpose, so hearing it out loud lands hard.

It's actually true, and Paul says it straight. He asks, “Do you wish to be enslaved by them all over again?” He's not scolding for fun. He's holding up a mirror so the Galatians can see what going back would mean.

Fears is it. Paul says, “I fear for you…” and that comes right after he lists the days and months and seasons and years. That's a man who's worried because he cares. A shrug would have been easier for him.
Prayer is a good thing, but Paul doesn't say it here. He says, “I fear for you…” That's honest and a little raw. He tells them straight what's on his heart.

Hope sounds nicer, but it's not the word on the page. Paul says, “I fear for you…” and that's the word that fits a man watching people he loves drift. He doesn't dress it up. I think that's why it hits so hard.

True. Paul says his fear is “…that my efforts for you may have been in vain.” He worked hard for these folks, and now he's worried it might not have stuck. I think anybody who's ever poured time into someone knows that ache.
Paul really does say it. He writes, “I fear for you, that my efforts for you may have been in vain.” He's not being dramatic. He's telling them how much this matters to him.

Not quite, friend. Paul says the opposite: “You have done me no wrong.” Right in the middle of all this worry, he makes sure they know there's no grudge. He's concerned, but he's not holding anything against them.
Right, it's false. Paul says, “You have done me no wrong.” He just begged them to become like him, and he wants them to know he's not angry. That's a big-hearted way to start a hard conversation.

Yes. Paul says, “You know that it was because of an illness that I first preached the gospel to you.” He doesn't hide it, and he doesn't make it fancy. Sometimes the story starts with a rough moment, and that's okay.
Shipwrecks make for a dramatic story, but Paul doesn't mention one here. He says it was “because of an illness.” He keeps it simple and honest about how he first came to them.
A big shaking would be a loud way to start, but Paul gives no earthquake here. He says, “…it was because of an illness that I first preached the gospel to you.” Quiet reason, big message.

explanations.answer: As if he were an angel of God
explanations.explanation: That's what Paul says. They “welcomed me as if I were an angel of God…” and he adds, “as if I were Christ Jesus Himself.” A sick man showed up, and they greeted him like that. I think that tells you how warm that first welcome was.

explanations.answer: As if he were a king of Israel
explanations.explanation: A king would get a parade, but Paul doesn't say that. He says they welcomed him “as if I were an angel of God, as if I were Christ Jesus Himself.” He was sick when he arrived, and they still treated him that well.

explanations.answer: As if he were a long lost brother
explanations.explanation: Brother is warm, but it's not what Paul writes. He says they “welcomed me as if I were an angel of God…” That's an even bigger welcome. And they gave it while he was sick.

True. Paul says they welcomed him “as if I were Christ Jesus Himself.” Think about that. A sick traveler walks in, and they treat him like that. It's the kind of welcome I'd have fallen over for after my drawer years.
Paul really does say it. After the angel of God, he adds, “as if I were Christ Jesus Himself.” He's reminding them how big their welcome was. That's what makes his question next hurt so much.

Eyes it is. Paul says, “…if it were possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me.” Notice the “if it were possible.” He's saying how deep their care ran, so I think he wants them to remember it.
Homes would be a generous gift, but Paul doesn't say homes. He says, “…if it were possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me.” Eyes are a lot closer to a person than a house.
Land is a big thing to give, but it's not on the page. Paul says they would have “torn out your eyes and given them to me.” That's about as personal as a gift can get.

Enemy is the word. Paul asks, “Have I now become your enemy by telling you the truth?” He's hurt, I think, because they once treated him like an angel. Now the truth makes him feel like the bad guy, and it stings.
Judge is close in feeling, but it's not Paul's word. He asks, “Have I now become your enemy by telling you the truth?” That's a sharper word, and it shows how much the change hurt him.
Servant isn't what he says. Paul asks whether telling the truth has made him their “enemy.” After the way they once welcomed him, that's a tender question. I think he really wants to know.

Right. Paul says, “…they want to isolate you from us, so that you may be zealous for them.” See the pattern? Cut off the Galatians from Paul and his friends, and then they're all theirs. It's like someone moving you to a quiet table so only they can talk to you.
Money never comes up in this passage. Paul says, “…they want to isolate you from us, so that you may be zealous for them.” Their goal is getting the Galatians' devotion, not their wallets.

explanations.answer: Hand them over to the rulers
explanations.explanation: Nothing about rulers is in these verses. Paul says those people “want to isolate you from us, so that you may be zealous for them.” It's about pulling the Galatians away from Paul and his friends.

True. Paul says they want to isolate the Galatians “so that you may be zealous for them.” Their goal is to make the Galatians care about them most. I think Paul sees it clearly, and he wants the Galatians to see it too.
It's true, and Paul says it plainly. Those people want to isolate the Galatians from Paul and his friends “so that you may be zealous for them.” He's pointing out where their zeal is aimed.
Not quite. Paul says the opposite: “…it is good to be zealous if it serves a noble purpose…” His problem isn't zeal itself. It's what that zeal is for.
Right. Paul says, “…it is good to be zealous if it serves a noble purpose…” So zeal can be a fine thing. The question he's raising is what it serves.

explanations.answer: At any time and not just when he's with them
explanations.explanation: Yes. Paul says it's good to be zealous for a noble purpose, “…at any time, and not only when I am with you.” In other words, don't just shine when the teacher's in the room. Keep going when nobody's watching.

explanations.answer: Only when he is there with them in person
explanations.explanation: That's actually the opposite. Paul says, “…at any time, and not only when I am with you.” He doesn't want their zeal to depend on him showing up. It should stay steady even when he's far away.

explanations.answer: Only when they meet together to pray
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't limit it to prayer meetings. He says it's good to be zealous for a noble purpose “…at any time, and not only when I am with you.” At any time covers a lot more ground than one gathering.

Childbirth is what Paul says. He writes, “My children, for whom I am again in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in you.” That's a picture of deep, hard-working love. Nobody says it about people they don't care about.
Fasting isn't the word. Paul says, “My children, for whom I am again in the pains of childbirth…” That's one of the strongest pictures of love and struggle he could pick.
Mourning is a sad word, but Paul doesn't use it here. He says he is “again in the pains of childbirth.” Those pains are about bringing something new to life, which is a very different picture.

True. Paul says he's in those pains “until Christ is formed in you.” He doesn't give a finish line other than that. He keeps caring until Christ is formed in them, and I think that says a lot about his heart.
It's true. Paul says, “…I am again in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in you.” That's how long he says he'll keep at it. He isn't giving up on them.

His tone, yes. Paul says, “…how I wish I could be with you now and change my tone, because I am perplexed about you.” I think a letter is hard because you can't see a face while you say a hard thing. In person, he wishes he could soften how it sounds.
Travel plans aren't what he mentions. Paul says he wishes he could be with them “and change my tone.” He's talking about how his words come across, not where he's going.
The message stays put. Paul says he wishes he could be with them “and change my tone.” That means how he says it, not what he says. He still tells the Galatians the truth.
